title: Beard Styles for a Round Face: How Long to Actually Grow Each One

tables.caption: Beard lengths for a round face — set the dial or the guard to the third column
head: Where it goes
Tool
Length
What that number buys you
rows: Razor, or trimmer with no comb
The strongest version of any style below. Nothing sits at the widest point, so all the length you grow reads as length.
Short enough that the beard does not tie itself into the haircut, long enough that the transition does not read as an accident.
Upper cheek, if you keep any
The lowest band that still looks deliberate rather than like day two. Under it, cheek growth reads as a patch that failed to fill.
Where a fade starts. Set the dial here and step down as you work up toward the sideburn.
Roughly double the cheek setting, applied where the face turns its corner. That doubling is the whole tightening effect.
The shortest length that still does the job here, and the one to start from if you have never grown a beard on purpose.
One guard longer than the cheeks. Enough to square the chin off without the beard developing a silhouette of its own.
Two guards longer than the cheeks. This is the gap that pulls the eye down the middle of the face instead of around it.
The longest setting worth trying on this outline, and only with the cheeks still held at 3 mm. Past it the beard outweighs the face it is on.
Level with the chin zone or shorter, and cut flat across rather than dressed downward at the corners.
tables.footnote: Guard fractions are the sizes Wahl stamps on its combs: #1 = 1/8 in, #2 = 1/4 in, #3 = 3/8 in, #4 = 1/2 in, #5 = 5/8 in, #8 = 1 in. Decimal inches are conversions at 25.4 mm to the inch. Rows under 1.6 mm have no guard.
